title: Career roadmap · AI Ethics Researcher
summary: Build from philosophy, social science and AI fundamentals into empirical AI ethics, algorithmic accountability, safety, governance, human rights and responsible technology research.

facts.Timeline assumption: The roadmap assumes a 2026-start Ph.D. pathway. Early years combine AI/ML literacy with philosophy, social science, law and research methods; later years focus on empirical evaluation, governance frameworks, technology policy and research leadership.

horizons.question: What can I enter now?
horizons.output: Build foundations in AI, philosophy of technology, ethics, social science, statistics, research methods and AI governance.

horizons.question: How should I specialise?
horizons.output: Establish a research niche such as algorithmic fairness, AI safety, privacy, human-AI interaction, AI governance or technology ethics.

horizons.question: How should I evolve?
horizons.output: Lead multidisciplinary research combining technical evaluation, normative analysis, law, policy and social impact.

horizons.question: How can I remain relevant?
horizons.output: Shape AI governance and responsible-AI research as models, agents, autonomous systems and regulatory environments evolve.

blocks.text: NIST's AI Risk Management Framework is designed around managing AI risks across development, deployment and evaluation, while UNESCO's framework emphasizes human dignity, human rights, fairness, human oversight and ethical impact assessment. These are useful reference points, but neither should be treated as a substitute for jurisdiction-specific law or institutional ethics review. NIST

blocks.text: Ph.D. routes

The senior AI-ethics researcher should operate across technical AI research, normative ethics, law, policy and institutional governance. AI systems will continue to change faster than many formal rules, so durable expertise comes from understanding underlying risks—fairness, privacy, safety, accountability, human agency and power—as well as the technical mechanisms that produce them. UNESCO's framework explicitly treats AI ethics as multidisciplinary and emphasizes human rights, impact assessment, governance, data policy and accountability; OECD principles similarly frame trustworthy AI around human rights and democratic values.
